title: Col. Robert Patterson builds Lexington
summary: In April 1779 Robert Patterson led about twenty-five men from Harrodsburg and began the fort at Lexington, then helped lay off the town.
bodyMarkdown:
Robert Patterson (1753–1827) was a Pennsylvania-born soldier and settler who helped found Lexington, Kentucky, and Cincinnati, Ohio. He [came to Kentucky in 1775](https://grokipedia.com/page/robert_patterson_%28pioneer%29). The [Kentucky Historical Society's marker](https://history.ky.gov/markers/patterson-cabin) adds that he was a large landholder who also took part in founding Dayton.

## A name before a town

The name Lexington came before Patterson's fort. [the history of Lexington](https://grokipedia.com/page/Lexington,_Kentucky) says frontiersmen under William McConnell named the site in June 1775. They had just heard about the fighting at Lexington, Massachusetts, on April 19, 1775, which opened the Revolutionary War. You can read more in [how Lexington got its name](/stories/lexington-named/).

## Building the fort in 1779

Permanent settlement began in April 1779. The KHS marker says Patterson chose the site, helped put up the fort and laid off the town. He [picked the spot](https://grokipedia.com/page/Lexington,_Kentucky) for defense and for its water and farmland. John Maxwell and [Levi Todd](/stories/levi-todd-lexington-co-founder/) were [among the men who raised the log stockade](https://grokipedia.com/page/Lexington,_Kentucky) and cabins.

Patterson served on the town's board of trustees for many years. He also helped charter Transylvania University.

## A militia officer in wartime

Patterson served in the Kentucky militia during the Revolutionary War. In 1778 he took part in George Rogers Clark's Illinois campaign. He was a captain of Fayette County militia at the [Battle of Blue Licks](/stories/battle-of-blue-licks/), the last major battle of the war in the West. He and Daniel Boone were among the few senior officers to survive that defeat.

The fighting with Native nations continued after the Revolution. In 1786 Patterson was badly wounded in [Logan's Raid](/stories/moluntha-and-logans-raid-1786/) during the Northwest Indian War.

## Politics and a move north

The marker says Patterson urged Kentucky's separation from Virginia in 1784. He was elected to represent Fayette County in 1792 and served eight years. In 1788 he moved into the Northwest Territory, where he became one of the three founders of Cincinnati.

He later settled near Dayton, Ohio. His farm, Rubicon, lay two miles south of the town, where he and his wife Elizabeth Lindsay raised eight children. During the War of 1812 he served as a quartermaster. His grandson John H. Patterson founded the National Cash Register Company in 1884.

## Kentucky today

Patterson built a small cabin before he married Elizabeth Lindsay in April 1780. It has served as a home, servants' quarters and tool shed and has stood in many places, including a Patterson grandson's farm at Dayton from 1901 to 1939. It was returned to Lexington and now stands on the Transylvania University campus near Third Street and Broadway.
